extracted.intended_audience: poets, students of poetry, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria for judging and producing poetry (diction, imagery, meter, characterization) focusing on the debate over using 'rustic' or 'real' language vs. polished poetic style. Useful for poets and critics deciding diction, metre, and character-representation strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of manner over novelty of subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Superior excellence in the manner of treating the same subjects was the trial and test of the artist's merit; novelty of subject was rather avoided than sought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy with painting: like the old masters who recycled the same motifs, poets should focus on the quality of treatment (polish, arrangement, expression) rather than inventing novel subjects. Anti-pattern: privileging novelty of subject at the expense of how it's handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of general, shared imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagery is almost always general; sun, moon, flowers, breezes, murmuring streams, warbling songsters, lovely damsels, nymphs, naiads, and goddesses are common materials which each poet shapes and arranges according to judgment or fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets may rely on common natural and mythic images, shaping them by arrangement and treatment. Novel images are not necessary if the handling is excellent. Example: many 15th–18th century poets used similar stock imagery and derived attraction from manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish of diction combined with perfect simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: The excellence at which they aimed consisted in the exquisite polish of the diction, combined with perfect simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rules derived: avoid words a gentleman would not use in dignified conversation and words only a learned man would use; study the position of words and phrases so each part is melodious and contributes to the harmony of the whole. Anti-patterns: needless learnedisms or vulgarisms that break harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melodious ordering and harmonic unity of phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Not only each part should be melodious in itself, but contribute to the harmony of the whole, each note referring and conducing to the melody of all the foregoing and following words of the same period or stanza.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange diction metrically and syntactically so lines/phrases interlock musically. The aim is pervasive melodic effect rather than isolated prettiness; watch word-order and cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrical variety via subtle modification of common metres
rubrics_metrics.description: The elder bards produced variety by countless modifications and subtle balances of sound in the common metres of their country, rather than by introducing new overpowering metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer nuanced variation within native metrical practice. Anti-pattern: borrowing foreign metres (e.g., German) whose mechanism enforces an overpowering tune that distracts readers into humming the metre rather than attending to meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of imported/overpowering metres
rubrics_metrics.description: New metres borrowed from the German, having in their very mechanism a specific overpowering tune, make readers humor their voice and emphasis with more indulgence to the author than attention to the meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious introducing unfamiliar metrical schemes that impose a strong, distracting rhythm. If meaning becomes subordinate to tune, the metre is counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to unite classical finish with deeper feeling and fresher imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: A lasting reputation awaits one who recalls high finish, appropriateness, facility, delicate proportion, and omnipresent grace of classical models, and combines these with keener interest, deeper pathos, manlier reflection, and fresher and more various imagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for synthesis: classical technical excellence plus modern depth and variety of feeling and image. Scoring note: works that achieve both polish and substantive emotional/reflective content are valued highly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is essentially ideal and generic
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry as poetry is essentially ideal: it avoids and excludes all accidents; apparent individualities of rank, character, or occupation must be representative of a class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters in poetry should embody generic/class attributes (the common attributes of the class) rather than idiosyncratic accidental details. Anti-pattern: over-specific individual quirks that undermine the poem's representative or instructive function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must have verisimilitude and representative quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons of poetry must be clothed with generic attributes such that they are persons of a known and abiding class, and their manners and sentiments the natural product of circumstances common to the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure plausibility that character behavior and language plausibly arise from the class' common conditions. Example: Michael's independence, frugality, and education explain his speech and conduct; scoring should reward representative plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select diction appropriate to genre and class — Wordsworth's 'real language' is limited
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that proper poetic diction consists altogether in language taken from the mouths of men in real life (especially low and rustic life) is applicable only to certain classes of poetry, and even then is often impracticable or injurious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not universally apply rustic/conversational diction to all poetry. Consider genre, purpose, and whether rustic language supplies the necessary generality and reflective vocabulary. Anti-pattern: wholesale imitation of 'rustic' speech across poetic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rustic language has limited vocabulary for abstract/reflected thought
rubrics_metrics.description: A rustic's distinct knowledge would furnish a very scanty vocabulary for reflective and discriminating expression; the best part of language is derived from reflection on the acts of the mind itself, not merely from objects with which rustics commune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer diction capable of expressing abstract, relational, and intellectual concepts when poem requires it; do not mistake familiarity with natural objects for sufficiency of poetic language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purify and adapt rustic/provincial speech if used
rubrics_metrics.description: The language of rustic life 'purified' from provincialism and grossness and made consistent with grammatical rules would not differ from the language of other educated men; many omissions and changes are required before rustic speech can be adapted to most poetic purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using colloquial/rustic elements, edit out provincialism and grossness and reorganize syntax to serve poetic ends. Anti-pattern: verbatim reproduction of dialectal garrulity that weakens poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imitating dull/garrulous discourse in lyric poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: In a lyric poem (and often in other poetic forms) it is not possible to imitate truly a dull and garrulous discouser without repeating the effects of dulness and garrulity, which harm poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not slavishly reproduce tedium or incoherence of ordinary speakers; where a narrator is meant to be dull, balance with poet's own imaginative passages. Example: parts better as poet's voice give universal delight; strictly garrulous passages may cause 'unpleasant sinkings'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion amplifies pre-existing language stock; it does not create diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever new connections or generalizations heat of passion may produce, the terms of their conveyance must have pre-existed in the speaker's former conversation; passion activates but does not invent the vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the speaker/poet plausibly possesses the verbal resources used during passion; do not rely on passion as an excuse for introducing felicitous language without prior acquisition. Anti-pattern: attributing sophisticated phrasing to a character lacking the background to have those words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic composition is distinct from prose and requires organized arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an essential difference between the language/order of prose and that of metrical composition: poetic composition should be prospectively organized, subordinating parts so as to convey an organized whole rather than the disjoined succession characteristic of uneducated conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange poems with foresight of overall structure and subordinate parts according to relative importance; value compactness and economy of expression over disjointed conversational order. Anti-pattern: composing verse that merely mimics the loose order of casual speech without poetic organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition as a high poetic beauty when fitting passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetitions (e.g., 'At her feet he bowed, he fell, he lay down; at her feet he bowed, he fell') can be a beauty of the highest kind when they illustrate intense and turbulent feeling where passion endures longer than a single representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repetition deliberately to convey sustained or heightened feeling; distinguish effective, artful repetition from mere tautology or filler. Example: Biblical verse (Song of Deborah) cited as exemplary.
